questions.q: In Problem 1, what is the verified circuit (starting from |00⟩) that produces (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2?
options: X on qubit 2, then H on qubit 1, then CNOT with control = q1, target = q2
H on qubit 1, then H on qubit 2, with no CNOT at all
X on qubit 1, then CNOT with control = q1, target = q2, with no H gate
H on qubit 1, then CNOT with control = q2, target = q1
questions.explain: Starting qubit 2 from |1⟩ (via X) before the standard H+CNOT recipe shifts the output from the 'qubits agree' pattern (|00⟩,|11⟩) to the 'qubits disagree' pattern (|01⟩,|10⟩), verified step by step to land on [0, 0.7071, 0.7071, 0].

questions.q: In Problem 2, a circuit applies H to each of 3 independent qubits (q1, q2, q3) and then a single CNOT with control = q1, target = q2. What are its width and depth?
options: Width 3, depth 2
Width 3, depth 3
Width 2, depth 2
Width 3, depth 1
questions.explain: Width is 3 (three qubits used). Depth is 2: all three H gates act on disjoint qubits and share layer 1, but the CNOT depends on q1 and q2's post-H states and must be layer 2; q3's H has nothing after it, so it doesn't extend the depth further.

questions.q: Why doesn't qubit 3's Hadamard gate in Problem 2 add any extra depth beyond the CNOT's layer?
options: Because qubit 3's H gate has no gate after it that depends on it, so it stays contained within layer 1 regardless of what happens on other qubits in layer 2
Because qubit 3 is not actually part of the circuit's width
Because H gates never count toward depth under any circumstance
Because CNOT implicitly also acts on qubit 3 even though it isn't drawn on that wire
questions.explain: Depth is set by the longest dependency chain. Qubit 3's chain is just one gate long (its H, with nothing following it), which is shorter than q1/q2's two-gate chain (H then CNOT) — so the overall depth is determined by q1/q2's chain, not q3's.

questions.q: In Problem 3, which circuit (starting from |00⟩) is verified to produce (|00⟩ − |01⟩ − |10⟩ + |11⟩)/2?
options: X on both qubits (reaching |11⟩), then H on qubit 1, then H on qubit 2, with no CNOT
H on qubit 1, then CNOT with control = q1, target = q2
X on qubit 1 only, then H on qubit 1, then H on qubit 2
H on both qubits starting directly from |00⟩, with no X gates
questions.explain: Starting from |11⟩ and applying H to each qubit independently was verified step by step to give [0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0.5], exactly (|00⟩-|01⟩-|10⟩+|11⟩)/2 — each qubit's H contributes a minus sign on its own |1⟩ component, so terms with exactly one bit equal to 1 (|01⟩, |10⟩) end up negative.

questions.q: What does Problem 3 illustrate that contrasts with Problems 1 and 2's use of CNOT?
options: A target state can use all four basis states with a nontrivial sign pattern and still be fully separable, requiring no entangling gate at all
Every target state with more than one nonzero amplitude always requires at least one CNOT
CNOT is only useful for producing exactly two nonzero amplitudes, never four
H gates alone can never produce a superposition over more than two basis states
questions.explain: Problem 3's target has four nonzero, equal-magnitude amplitudes with a specific sign pattern, yet it was reached with two independent H gates and no CNOT — demonstrating that entanglement and 'using many basis states' are not the same thing, and recognizing when a CNOT isn't needed is part of the design skill.
